about.title: Murrieta Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Murrieta's workforce is spread across warehouses, medical offices, construction sites, retail along Winchester Road, and a steady stream of people who drive for a living in and around Riverside County. When one of those jobs leaves you hurt, the first question is usually simple: who pays? In California, workers' compensation covers most on-the-job injuries no matter who was at fault, and it is normally your only route against your employer. The picture changes when someone outside your company caused the harm. A subcontractor who left a hazard on a Clinton Keith Road jobsite, a manufacturer whose equipment failed, or another driver who struck you while you were making deliveries can each face a separate injury claim with its own two-year deadline. That distinction matters in a city of roughly 109,830 residents where, in 2025, 426 injury collisions left 595 people hurt, and anyone driving for work shares those same roads. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect you with an independent attorney who reviews your situation and works on contingency.

items.title: Retaliation is illegal, and you are not alone

items.question: I was hit on Murrieta Hot Springs Road while driving for work. Is workers' comp my only option?
items.answer: Probably not. Because you were on the job, workers' compensation should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of fault. If another driver caused the crash, that driver is a third party, and California allows a separate injury claim against them with a two-year deadline. An attorney can pursue both without one canceling the other.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly for a workplace injury in California?
items.answer: In most situations, no. Workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer, even when the employer was careless. The exceptions are narrow, which is why the more common route to additional recovery is a claim against a negligent third party such as a contractor, property owner, or equipment manufacturer.

items.question: What if I waited a few weeks to report my injury to my Riverside County employer?
items.answer: Report it now, in writing. California gives you 30 days to notify your employer, and delays beyond that can complicate the comp claim, though they do not always end it. Any third-party injury claim runs on its own two-year timeline, so a late report to your boss does not automatically close that door.
